cells.tense: The pen is in your hand here, and the sorting is yours.
cells.ask: Name one promise you are keeping on purpose, not for what it gives back, and say out loud which pull you are letting go of for now. Sorting the possible feelings by hand decides it on purpose instead of by mood, and the table stays clear.
cells.core:
You know which pull in the room is real and which one is only loud, so you sort by hand rather than by mood. Nothing gets carried out of here half-finished, which means what leaves moves on clean and the bench is clear for the next thing.

The rule you go by is plain and it keeps the possible feelings from running the table: what comes close enough to change you stays, and what doesn't stays outside. Working it that way is the same as clearing the bench before the next one starts, and the room stays workable because you decided it would. What a promise needs from you is the sorting — and you are already doing it with the pen in your hand.

cells.tense: You are braced at a finish line the work hasn't reached.
cells.ask: Name one thing that is already finished and let it stand finished for today — no reopening, no new version. Holding what is complete gives the next thing solid ground to start from.
cells.core:
Gathering what is possible works here when you let each thing land finished — the door closes, you stand there a moment, and the next room gets a clean floor. That's finishing with your feet under you, and the bench clears itself.

Right now you're already three steps ahead of what's actually done, hunting the next version before this one lands. That rushing keeps you from seeing which thing is already over, so everything sits half-open and the leaving gets put off. Naming one finished thing lets it stand and gives the next one somewhere to start. That's the whole difference between gathering and hoarding — the finished thing is allowed to be finished.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.ask: Say one true sentence about what you want before you plan anything around it. Even if you don't say it to anyone, hearing your own voice put it in the room.
cells.core:
What you want is a thing you can say out loud and stand behind, and the room you're in is a room you keep. That's what arriving looks like here — the possible feelings become promises instead of a list, and the door behind you swings shut.

As it stands, the door is closed and you're on the far side of it. Nothing here registers as a claim you can make or refuse, so the feelings arrive as a list and stay one. One sentence in your own ears puts your feet back in the room, and the list becomes something you're standing in.

cells.tense: The pen is down but the room keeps moving as if it were still in your hand.
cells.ask: Write one sentence: 'The sorting ran on its own today.' Naming it makes the closing visible instead of automatic.
cells.core:
When you're in charge of it, the room opens and closes on purpose — some feelings come close enough to change you, some stay outside, and you know which is which because you said so. That's keeping this room from the inside, and the bench gets cleared by hand.

What's actually happening is that the sorting already runs. You pick what gets through and what stays outside whenever something comes near, and the story you tell is that the current is doing it. What your hands do with the possible feelings is the decision, and nobody has claimed it yet. Saying it once is what puts the pen back in your fingers. The work was yours from the start; the sentence is the only part that's missing.
